steps.title: What is the Water Cycle?
steps.description: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water on, above, and below the Earth's surface. Water moves upward as water vapor through evaporation and downward through precipitation (rain, snow, hail), passing through soil, rocks, and plants, and finally returning to water bodies.

steps.title: Evaporation: Water Rises
steps.description: When the Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes, it evaporates and becomes water vapor. The Sun's radiation provides the energy needed to convert liquid water into gas. Water also evaporates from trees and plants through a process called transpiration.

steps.title: Condensation: Clouds Form
steps.description: As water vapor rises up into the atmosphere, it cools down. When it cools enough, the water vapor condenses into tiny water droplets, forming clouds. This process is called condensation.

steps.title: Precipitation: Rain Falls
steps.description: When clouds become heavy with water droplets, they release the water back to Earth as precipitation - rain, snow, or hail. This water falls on the surface, replenishing water bodies.

steps.title: Collection & Infiltration
steps.description: Rainwater that falls on Earth either flows into ponds, lakes, rivers, and oceans, or seeps into the ground through infiltration. Water that infiltrates gets stored as groundwater in underground layers called aquifers.

steps.title: The Complete Cycle
steps.description: The water cycle helps redistribute and replenish water across Earth. It conserves the total amount of water on our planet through this continuous movement - evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.

steps.title: Real World: Drying Clothes
steps.description: Have you noticed wet clothes drying faster on sunny days? The Sun's heat causes water in the clothes to evaporate faster. This is the same evaporation process that happens in the water cycle! The Sun provides the energy needed to convert liquid water into water vapor.

steps.title: Real World: Morning Dew
steps.description: Early morning dew on grass is water cycle in action! During the night, water vapor in the air cools down and condenses on cool surfaces like grass and leaves. This is the same condensation process that forms clouds in the sky.

steps.title: Real World: Rainwater Harvesting
steps.description: In many parts of India, people collect rainwater using harvesting systems. This harvested water seeps into the ground, replenishing groundwater in aquifers. This demonstrates the collection and infiltration stage of the water cycle, helping ensure sustainable water supply.

steps.title: Real World: Ice Stupas in Ladakh
steps.description: In Ladakh, people create ice stupas - tall cone-shaped ice structures - by spraying water into cold air during winter. The water freezes layer by layer. In spring, these stupas melt slowly, providing water for farming. This innovative technique uses the water cycle principles of freezing (precipitation) and melting to solve water scarcity.

clothes.howItWorks: The Sun's heat causes water molecules in wet clothes to gain energy and evaporate. As water changes from liquid to vapor, it escapes into the air, leaving clothes dry.
clothes.scienceBehind: Evaporation occurs when water molecules absorb enough thermal energy to break free from liquid bonds. Solar radiation provides this energy, increasing molecular motion until molecules escape as vapor.
clothes.realExample: Every Indian household experiences this daily! Clothes hung in direct sunlight dry in 2-3 hours, while in shade they take 6-8 hours. During monsoon (cloudy), clothes take even longer as solar radiation is blocked.
benefits: Saves electricity - no need for clothes dryers
Natural disinfection - UV rays in sunlight kill bacteria
Clothes smell fresh from outdoor drying

dew.howItWorks: During the night, air temperature drops. When water vapor in the air comes into contact with cool surfaces (grass, leaves), it loses energy and condenses into liquid water droplets - forming dew.
dew.scienceBehind: Condensation occurs when water vapor cools below its dew point. Cool surfaces provide nucleation sites where water molecules can cluster together, forming visible droplets.
dew.realExample: Early morning dew is common across India, especially in regions like Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Farmers observe dew formation to understand local humidity and temperature patterns.
benefits: Provides moisture for plants in dry regions
Indicates high humidity and temperature patterns
Natural water source for small insects and animals

harvesting.howItWorks: Rainwater is collected from rooftops and directed into storage tanks or underground pits. The collected water then seeps into the ground through infiltration, replenishing groundwater aquifers.
harvesting.scienceBehind: Infiltration occurs when water moves downward through soil pores due to gravity. The rate depends on soil type, slope, and vegetation. Collected rainwater follows the same path as natural precipitation in the water cycle.
harvesting.realExample: In Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka, rainwater harvesting is mandatory for buildings. Traditional systems like 'tankas' in Rajasthan and 'kattas' in Karnataka demonstrate collection and infiltration principles.
benefits: Reduces flooding by storing excess rainwater

ice-stupa.howItWorks: Water is sprayed into freezing winter air, where it freezes layer by layer, forming cone-shaped ice structures. In spring, these stupas melt slowly, providing water for irrigation when needed most.
ice-stupa.scienceBehind: Freezing (solidification) occurs when water loses thermal energy and molecules slow down, forming ice crystals. Melting reverses this process. The cone shape maximizes volume while minimizing surface area, slowing melt rate.
ice-stupa.realExample: In Ladakh's Phyang village, ice stupas created by engineer Sonam Wangchuk provide water for farming during spring when natural sources are scarce. Some stupas store 2-3 million liters of water!
benefits: Solves water scarcity in cold desert regions
Provides water during critical farming season
Uses natural freezing - no energy required
Innovative adaptation of water cycle principles
